<reason>Side B (PRO) won a close, high-quality exchange. B answered both pressure questions concretely (B4.1's "redundancy plus time" mechanism for screening treatable despair; B4.3-4.4's entrenchment, sunset clauses, and diagnosis-keyed eligibility) and turned A's fallibility argument into a dilemma by noting that treatment refusal and palliative sedation run on the same fallible prognosis and competence judgments. B's "which policy produces more irreversible harm" reframing neutralized A's irreversibility asymmetry, and the closing leveraged A's own concession in [A4.3] that residual suffering persists even under ideal care into the decisive weighing: certain torment of the residual patient versus speculative harm. Side A (CON) genuinely won the Canada/slippery-slope clash—A4.4's turn that court-driven autonomy reasoning dissolved Canada's diagnosis-based line, and A5.1-5.3's "the premise is the solvent" crystallization, were excellent—but A's answers to B's pressure (A4.1's act/omission distinction) were more asserted than argued, and A never escaped the fallibility dilemma or engaged B's unaddressed displaced-suicide harm-reduction point. Both openings were clipped (equal execution cost). B made the debate easier to decide and left the stronger live route to victory on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1's answer to A's depression-screening pressure—time as the diagnostic instrument that separates fluctuating despair from progressive disease, plus the tu quoque that CON's own preferred regime rests on identical fallible judgments—paired with B5.1-5.3's exploitation of A4.3's concession. A's best counter was A4.4/A5.1: showing that the autonomy logic underpinning PRO's case was the very thing courts used to erase Canada's "strict" boundary.</best_rebuttal>
